abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: This work reports a novel one-pot hydrothermal synthesis of N-CQDs using Solanum nigrum L. as sustainable carbon source and triethylamine as nitrogen provider. The resulting N-CQDs were systematically characterized with TEM, SEM, FT-IR, XPS, XRD, and UV–Visible. Significantly, the N-CQDs exhibited substantial antimicrobial efficacy against both S. aureus and E. coli bacterial strains, with minimum inhibitory concentration values of 1.2 mg/mL and 1.1 mg/mL, respectively. Moreover, the N-CQDs demonstrated pronounced fluorescence enhancement upon interaction with ciprofloxacin, displaying exceptional selectivity and sensitivity, with a calculated LOD of 316 nM. The feasibility of employing N-CQDs as fluorescent probes for ciprofloxacin detection was systematically validated through practical application in honey analysis. This study introduces a novel approach for the fabrication of N-CQDs derived from natural botanical sources, underscoring their potential dual functionality as fluorescent sensors and antimicrobial materials.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Carbon Quantum dots (CQDs) have emerged as a highly advantageous class of nanomaterials compared to MOFs and COFs, particularly in terms of biocompatibility, synthetic simplicity, and multifunctional applications. CQDs can be prepared via straightforward hydrothermal or solvothermal methods using abundant and low-cost carbon sources such as biomass, pharmaceuticals, or even coal1,2. Additionally, CQDs exhibit superior photostability and tunable fluorescence without the need for intricate structural modifications3. In biomedical applications, CQDs demonstrate exceptional biocompatibility and low cytotoxicity, enabling real-time bioimaging and targeted drug delivery4,5. Their small size and abundant surface functional groups also facilitate rapid cellular uptake and efficient renal clearance6–9.

CQDs have emerged as a superior alternative to traditional analytical techniques such as electrochemistry and HPLC due to their exceptional fluorescence properties, high sensitivity, and biocompatibility. CQDs offer a label-free, rapid, and highly selective detection mechanism, requiring minimal sample preparation. For example, CQDs for detecting spermine with a detection limit of 52.7 nM, outperforming conventional HPLC in terms of sensitivity and cost-effectiveness. Additionally, CQD-based fluorescence assays enable real-time detection with excellent stability under varying pH and ionic conditions10,11. Moreover, CQDs demonstrate superior catalytic and anti-interference capabilities in complex matrices, such as biological fluids and environmental samples, where traditional methods often struggle with matrix effects. Thus, the integration of CQDs into fluorescence-based detection platforms represents a transformative advancement in analytical science, combining simplicity, high throughput, and unparalleled precision12.

In recent years, antimicrobial resistance has emerged as a critical global health concern, primarily driven by the proliferation of multidrug-resistant microorganisms, commonly referred to as “superbugs”13. This threat has been associated with substantial increases in both morbidity and mortality rates worldwide. Recent epidemiological analyses demonstrate a concerning mortality burden from antibiotic-resistant pathogens in the U.S., with current annual deaths estimated at 35,000 a significant increase from prior estimates, underscoring the accelerating threat to population health14. This escalating threat necessitates the development of novel therapeutic approaches to address bacterial infections beyond conventional antibiotics15–17. Comparative antibacterial studies reveal that CQDs achieve microbial inactivation via dual pathways light-induced ROS production (O₂•⁻, H₂O₂, •OH) causing oxidative damage, and electrostatic interaction-driven membrane penetration facilitated by their inherent positive surface charge18, capable of inducing oxidative damage to biomolecules. As key secondary messengers, these oxidative species modulate essential physiological processes, including stress adaptation and regulated cell death, through intricate crosstalk with cellular redox buffering mechanisms. The cationic surface charges of CQDs facilitate strong electrostatic attraction to anionic components of bacterial membranes, leading to the disruption of membrane integrity and subsequent decomposition of the bacterial cell membrane¹². Recently, many researchers have synthesized fluorescent probes with lower inhibitory concentrations against E. coli and S. aureus, With minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and minimal bactericidal concentration (MBC) values of 1.8 mg/mL across both bacterial types, honey-originated CQDs emerge as clinically promising antimicrobial agents, showing superior efficacy to conventionally synthesized carbon nanomaterials19. The methanol-soluble fraction of S. maritima exhibited significant growth inhibition, with MIC values of 25 mg/mL against E. coli and 6.25 mg/mL against S. aureus suggesting differential susceptibility between Gram-negative and Gram-positive pathogens20. Phytochemical analysis revealed that polyphenolic compounds from date syrup also exhibit distinct antimicrobial activity21. Notably, analytical characterization reveals that nitrogen-doped CQDs display superior bacteriostatic activity relative to conventional antimicrobial agents. Incorporating dopants into CQDs modifies their compositional and structural properties, leading to tailored electronic energy levels or states, which subsequently influences their functional performance across diverse applications22.

In addition, CQDs demonstrate exceptional suitability for luminescent sensing applications owing to their superior quantum efficiency, remarkable photochemical stability, and intrinsic resistance to chemical degradation23,24. As a fluoroquinolone-class antibiotic, ciprofloxacin (CIP) demonstrates primary therapeutic efficacy against uropathogenic bacterial infections25. However, supraphysiological administration may induce multisystemic complications including dermatological manifestations, hepatotoxicity, neurocognitive disturbances, and gastrointestinal dysfunction. Therefore, the accurate quantification of CIP is extremely important. However, conventional detection methods rely on expensive instruments and are time-consuming. Honey samples are even more difficult to detect due to their complex composition. Thus, a selective fluorescent sensor was employed for the accurate quantification of CIP. Photochemistry detection platforms offer distinct advantages in CIP monitoring through instrumentation-minimized protocols requiring minimal technical expertise26,27. CQDs exhibit particular promise in this regard, outperforming conventional fluorophores through enhanced biosafety profiles, reduced environmental footprint, and exceptional photobleaching resistance. Numerous studies have reported the development of fluorescent probes for CIP detection, among which a sensor based on CQDs derived from Cinnamomum Tamala exhibits a linear response range of 1-100 µ mol/L and a detection limit of 6.06 µ mol/L26. The blue-fluorescent CQDs, which synthesized using passionfruit shell, exhibited a strong linear response to CIP in aqueous solutions across a concentration range of 0–250 µmol/L, with a low detection limit of 0.86 µmol/L27. The synthesized CdSe functioned as a highly selective and sensitive fluorescence probe for CIP detection via a fluorescence resonance energy transfer mechanism. The sensor exhibited a linear response range of 0–120 µmol/L (R² = 0.9956) with a detection limit of 0.6 µmol/L28. The experimental findings unveil that N - CQDs present remarkably lower detection limits, a characteristic that holds great promise for advancing high - sensitivity detection technologies.

This study presents the first report on the synthesis of N-CQDs using Solanum nigrum L. and triethylamine as precursors via a one-step hydrothermal method, which adheres to green chemistry principles and is environmentally sustainable. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM), Scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Fourier - transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) and X - ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) were employed to comprehensively characterize the structural and chemical properties of the N - CQDs and X-ray diffraction (XRD) reflects the crystallinity of carbon dots through the position and intensity of diffraction peaks. The resulting N-CQDs displayed potent antibacterial activity against both S. aureus and E. coli. Moreover, N-CQDs demonstrated considerable potential as a fluorescent probe for the detection of CIP. This work introduces a novel strategy for fabricating multifunctional carbon-based nanomaterials with applications in clinical diagnostics and environmental monitoring.

sec.title: Materials
sec.p: Solanum nigrum L. were procured from a supermarket in Chongqing, China. All experimental procedures requiring aqueous solutions utilized deionized water. Phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH 7.4), coumarin-3-carboxylic acid (CCA), Luria-Bertani (LB) broth, and 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)−2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) were obtained from Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Additionally, Tris and HPA were sourced from Aladdin Reagent Co. (Shanghai, China). Microbial strains, including E. coli JM109 and S. aureus ATCC 6538, were acquired from Beijing Biotechnology Co., Ltd.

sec.title: Testing and characterization
sec.p: The structural characteristics of N-CQDs, including their nanoscale morphology and crystalline lattice arrangement, were examined using high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM, Tecnai G2 20, FEI, USA). Surface chemical states and elemental distribution were assessed via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., USA), while functional group identification was conducted through Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR, Thermo Scientific, USA). Additionally, optical absorption properties were evaluated by ultraviolet-visible (UV-vis) spectroscopy using an Evolution 220 spectrometer (Thermo Electron, USA). UV-vis spectroscopy was performed utilizing an Evolution 220 UV-visible spectrometer to obtain the spectral data. The photoluminescent emission characteristics of N-CQDs were analyzed using a fluorescence spectrophotometer (RF-5301PC, Shimadzu). Antimicrobial efficacy was quantitatively assessed via MIC determination, performed by monitoring optical density at 600 nm using a microplate reader (StatFax 4200, Awareness Technology). Furthermore, zeta potential testing was carried out to evaluate the surface charge, stability, and aggregation tendency of both the N-CQDs and bacteria.

sec.title: Preparation of N-CQDs
sec.p: The N-CQDs were synthesized via a one-step hydrothermal method. Briefly, 0.30 g of Solanum nigrum L. and triethylamine were dispersed in 15 mL of deionized water under stirring to ensure homogeneity. The mixture was then transferred into a 25 mL Teflon-lined autoclave and subjected to hydrothermal treatment at 120 °C for 6 h. After the reaction, the autoclave was allowed to cool to room temperature naturally. The resulting suspension was centrifuged at 8000 rpm for 10 min to remove large particles. The supernatant was further filtered through a 0.22 μm microporous membrane to obtain a clear solution. To purify the N-CQDs, the solution was dialyzed using a dialysis bag with a molecular weight cutoff of 500 Da for 12 h to remove any unreacted precursors or small impurities. Finally, the purified N-CQDs solution was freeze-dried to yield a solid powder, which was stored at 4 °C for subsequent characterization and applications.

sec.title: Culture of bacterial
sec.p: E. coli and S. aureus were cultured in LB broth medium under standard conditions. Each bacterial strain was inoculated into 5 mL of LB medium and incubated at 37 °C for 12 h with continuous shaking at 180 rpm to ensure optimal growth. The bacterial concentration was monitored by measuring the OD600, and cultures were maintained within an OD600 range of 0.6 to 0.8 to ensure consistent growth phases. The bacterial suspensions were then diluted to a final concentration of 1.5 × 10⁷ CFU/mL. Following activation, the bacterial suspensions were stored at 4 °C in a refrigerator for subsequent experimental use.

sec.title: Assay of antibacterial activity
sec.p: The MIC of N-CQDs against E. coli and S. aureus were determined by co-culturing 100 µL aliquots of diluted bacterial suspensions with equal volumes of gradient N-CQDs solutions in 96-well plates. Post-axenic incubation (37 °C, 12 h static culture), microbial biomass density was spectrophotometrically assessed at λ = 600 nm using a pre-calibrated standard curve. Subsequently, to verify the metabolic activity, 10 µL of MTT reagent was added to each well and allowed to incubate for 20 min. Dose-response relationships were graphically represented as bacterial growth inhibition curves. For time-dependent antibacterial evaluation, bacterial suspensions (1 × 106 to 1 × 107 CFU/mL) were exposed to varying N-CQDs concentrations in 10 mL centrifuge tubes under shaking conditions (37 ℃, 24 h). To evaluate the time-dependent antibacterial efficacy of N-CQDs, OD600 were recorded for varying concentrations over time.

sec.title: Antibacterial mechanism
sec.p: Equal volumes of the activated bacterial suspension and diluted N-CQDs solution were homogenized by vortex mixing, followed by continuous agitation at 37 °C for 12 h in an orbital shaker incubator (180 rpm). Following incubation, the surface charge characteristics of the suspension were assessed through zeta potential measurements. The hydroxyl radical (•OH) generation capacity of the N-CQDs was quantitatively analyzed using fluorescence spectroscopy.

sec.title: Stability assay of N-CQDs
sec.p: As shown in Figure S1, the photobleaching resistance of N-CQDs was systematically evaluated through continuous UV irradiation (330 nm, 60 min). Fluorescence stability was subsequently assessed under simulated harsh conditions, including a broad pH spectrum (1.89–11.98) and solutions containing elevated concentrations of hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂, 0.6 mM) and sodium chloride (NaCl, 4 mM).

sec.title: Sensitivity and selective detection
sec.p: To evaluate the binding selectivity of N-CQDs, aliquots of the N-CQDs solution were introduced into separate 100 mM solutions containing various target analytes, including different ionic species, antibiotics, and amino acids. The resulting mixtures were then equilibrated at ambient temperature (25 ± 2 °C) for 1 h prior to analysis. Following 1-hour incubation, fluorescence spectra were acquired using 330 nm excitation. Furthermore, to assess the detection sensitivity, a concentration-dependent analysis was performed using trace-level CIP solutions ranging from 0 to 4 µ M. Triplicate measurements ensured data reproducibility. Experiments were carried out in an environment where temperature was allowed to equilibrate with the surrounding conditions.

sec.title: Quantum yield (QY) calculation
sec.p: Quinine sulfate in 0.1 M H2SO4 (QY%= 54, η = 1.33) selected as a standard to calculate the QY of N-CQDs29.

where φst is the known quantum yield of quinine sulfate, Kx and Ky are the integrated areas of the emission of N-CQDs and quinine sulfate, Ax and Ay are the UV-absorbance of the sample and the reference, and η is the refractive index of solvent (water: 1.33). The fluorescence quantum yield was 12.7%.

sec.title: Characterization of N-CQDs
sec.p: The N-CQDs were fabricated through a single-step hydrothermal synthesis approach. The morphology, functional groups, and surface composition of the N-CQDs were systematically characterized using FTIR, TEM, XPS and XRD. As shown in Fig. 1a, TEM analysis revealed well-dispersed spherical nanoparticles with narrow size distribution, exhibiting diameters ranging from 2.35 to 5.60 nm and average diameter size of 3.77 nm. HRTEM analysis provided clear evidence of well - defined lattice fringes within the N - CQDs. These lattice fringes exhibited an interplanar spacing precisely measured at 0.14 nm30. This study further analyzed the crystal structure of N-CQDs through XRD, as shown in Fig. 1b. The XRD pattern of N-CQDs shows a broad peak at 2 θ ≈ 26°, attributed to the disordered carbon of graphene31.

caption.p: (a) TEM image of the N-CQDs and the insets show the particle size distribution and the HRTEM images. (b) XRD image of N-CQDs. (c) FT-IR spectrum of N-CQDs. (d) XPS survey spectrum of N-CQDs. High-resolution XPS spectra of (e) O1s, (f) N1s, (g) C1s.

sec.p: FTIR spectroscopy was employed to characterize the surface functional groups of the N-CQDs, as illustrated in Fig. 1c. The FTIR spectrum of the purified N-CQDs exhibited distinct absorption peaks at 3376 cm⁻¹, 1584 cm⁻¹, 1397 cm⁻¹, 1034 cm⁻¹, and 802 cm⁻¹. The stretching vibrations of O–H/N-H bonds were identified as the origin of the absorption peak at 3376 cm⁻¹. Meanwhile, the peak detected at 1584 cm⁻¹ was assigned to the stretching vibrations of C = O bonds. Additionally, the absorption band at 802 cm⁻¹ was found to represent the vibrations of C–H bonds. Furthermore, spectral analysis identified characteristic vibrational modes at 1397 cm⁻¹, attributable to C-N bond stretching, along with a broad absorption band at 1034 cm⁻¹ corresponding to C-O vibrational stretching32.

The surface functionalization of N-CQDs was systematically characterized through XPS analysis. As depicted in Fig. 1d, the elemental survey scan confirmed the coexistence of carbon, oxygen, and nitrogen species. High-resolution deconvolution of the O 1 s spectrum (Fig. 1e) revealed three distinct components at 533.4 eV, 532.5 and 531.9 eV, corresponding to ether-type oxygen (C-O-C), carbonyl groups (C = O), and amide group (O = C-N) respectively. The N 1 s spectral profile (Fig. 1f) exhibited three resolved peaks at 401.9 eV, 399.8 eV, and 397.2 eV, which were assigned to secondary amine group (C-N-C), pyrrolic nitrogen, and primary amine group(R-NH2). Further analysis of the C 1 s spectrum (Fig. 1g) displayed characteristic binding energies at 288.5 eV, 286.4 eV, and 284.8 eV, indicative of carbonyl groups (C = O), carbon nitrogen single bond (C-N), and carbon-carbon double bond (C = C), respectively33. This comprehensive XPS investigation revealed the presence of multiple surface functional groups, a finding that showed remarkable consistency with FTIR spectroscopic data.

sec.title: Antibacterial activity of N-CQDs
sec.p: MTT staining, a method for detecting viable cells based on mitochondrial activity, was employed to indirectly assess cellular proliferation activity. The antimicrobial performance of N-CQDs was assessed using S. aureus and E. coli as model bacterial strains to represent distinct classes of pathogenic microorganisms. Bacterial suspensions were exposed to gradient concentrations of N-CQDs and Solanum nigrum L solution for 12 h prior to MTT analysis34. The comparison results showed that the antibacterial performance of N-CQDs against these two strains was superior to that of eggplant solution. As illustrated in Fig. 2a and b, the MICs of N-CQDs against E. coli and S. aureus were determined to be 1.2 g/mL and 1.1 g/mL, respectively.

caption.p: (a) The antibacterial ability of N-CQDs on E. coli and (b) S. aureus.

sec.p: Figure 3a and b demonstrate complete growth inhibition of both bacterial strains within 24 h at N-CQDs concentrations corresponding to 1×MIC and 2×MIC. The quantitative analysis distinctly showed that the antibacterial activity against S. aureus was considerably more potent than that against E. coli. correlating well with MTT assay data. Furthermore, serial passage experiments over 14 generations showed no statistically significant alteration in MIC values (Fig. 3c), confirming the absence of detectable resistance development in either bacterial strain.

caption.p: (a) Inhibitory effect on E. coli and (b) S. aureus of different concentrations of N-CQDs. (c) The study of N-CQDs on the resistance of E. coli and S. aureus. (d) The generated ROS of N-CQDs Hydroxyl radicals. (e) Zeta potential distribution of N-CQDs.

sec.title: Antibacterial mechanism of N-CQDs
sec.p: Fluorescence spectral analysis (Fig. 3d) revealed a marked enhancement in emission intensity at 450 nm following N-CQDs exposure, indicative of hydroxyl radical (•OH) generation. This fluorescence amplification provides direct evidence of the oxidative species production capability of N-CQDs35. Zeta potential measurements (Fig. 3e) demonstrated distinct surface charge characteristics, with S. aureus (−28.19 ± 0.41 mV) and E. coli (−17.83 ± 0.35 mV) exhibiting native negative surface potentials, contrasting with the positive surface charge of N-CQDs (+ 21.6 ± 1.2 mV). Following N-CQDs treatment, both bacterial strains displayed a modest but consistent increase in zeta potential values (S. aureus: −22.4 ± 0.8 mV; E. coli: −14.2 ± 0.6 mV), suggesting effective surface charge modulation through N-CQDs adsorption.

SEM analysis was employed to investigate the morphological alterations of bacterial cells following N-CQDs treatment (Fig. 4). Comparative observations revealed that untreated control groups of Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus maintained intact cellular structures with well-defined cell walls. In contrast, N-CQDs-treated specimens exhibited severe morphological disruptions, including cell wall deformation and membrane disintegration, ultimately resulting in bacterial lethality.

caption.p: SEM images of E. coli (a) and S. aureus (c) without N-CQDs treatment, as well as E. coli (b) and S. aureus (d) treated with N-CQDs.

sec.title: Fluorescence properties of N-CQDs
sec.p: Under ambient lighting conditions, the newly synthesized N-CQDs manifested as a yellow, translucent solution. Upon irradiation with 365 nm ultraviolet (UV) light, these N-CQDs emitted a subtle green fluorescent glow. In addition, the fluorescence quantum yield was calculated to be 12.7%. As depicted in Fig. 5a, the UV-Vis absorption spectrum of the synthesized N-CQDs features a distinct absorption peak at 270 nm. This peak can be attributed to the π–π* transition taking place at the boundaries of the carbon lattice structure36. Spectrofluorometric analysis revealed peak excitation at 330 nm with corresponding emission maxima at 439 nm. Fluorescence emission profiles of the N-CQDs solutions were systematically recorded across an excitation spectrum spanning 300–550 nm, as presented in Fig. 5b.

caption.p: (a) Spectral characterization of N-CQDs showing excitation/emission profiles and UV-vis absorption spectrum. (b) Excitation wavelength-dependent fluorescence emission spectra. Insets display photographic images of N-CQDs aqueous solutions under visible light (left) and 365 nm UV irradiation (right), demonstrating their optical properties.

sec.p: Furthermore, the N-CQDs demonstrated remarkable stability. As depicted in Figure S1, under diverse experimental setups and environmental factors, the N-CQDs’ fluorescence intensity persisted with little to no significant alteration, indicating robust photostability. These findings indicate that the N-CQDs possess strong resistance to photobleaching, as well as excellent stability against acidic, alkaline, saline, and oxidative environments.

sec.title: Selectivity of N-CQDs to CIP
sec.p: To investigate the selectivity of N-CQDs toward a range of analytes, including antibiotics, amino acids, and ions, fluorescence-based sensing experiments were conducted. During these studies, a notable phenomenon was observed: N-CQDs exhibited a specific and significant fluorescence enhancement in the presence of CIP. As vividly depicted in Fig. 6a and b, theN-CQDs treated with CIP were the sole specimens to exhibit a pronounced fluorescence enhancement, standing out distinctly from other tested samples (namely Chloramphenicol, Furazolidone, Streptomycin, Amoxicillin, Doxycycline, Metronidazole, Glucose, Tetracycline, Roxithromycin and Terramycin), amino acids (namely Proline, Leucine, Lysine, Alanine, Phenylalanine, Glycine, Tryptophan, Arginine Leucine, and Valine) and ions (namely Br-, C2H3O2-, PO43-, CN-, F-, NO3-, Cl-, S2-, Br-, H2PO4-, HPO42-, IO3-, Ca2+, Al3+, Sn2+, K+, Fe3+, Ba2+, Cu2+,Na+) did not change significantly37. These results demonstrate the selective binding affinity of N-CQDs toward CIP.

caption.p: (a) FL response to various antibiotics, amino acids and (b) ions. (c) The FL response of N-CQDs to different CIP concentrations. (d) The relationship between CIP concentration and (F – F0)/F0, where F is the FL intensity in the presence of the target CIP and F0 is the FL intensity in the blank group. Inset: linear relationship in the range of 0.1–1 µmol/L. (e) UV-vis absorption spectra of N-CQDs, CIP and N-CQDs/CIP.

sec.p: To systematically evaluate the fluorescence sensing performance of N-CQDs toward CIP, a concentration-dependent fluorescence response analysis was performed across 0–4 µmol/L CIP gradients. Figure 6c demonstrates a progressive fluorescence enhancement proportional to CIP concentration increments. Figure 6d reveals a highly linear correlation (R² = 0.9991) between the signal enhancement efficiency and CIP concentration across the 0.1-1 µM range. The detection sensitivity was exceptionally high, with a calculated limit of detection (LOD) of 316 nM (3σ/k, in which σ corresponds to the standard error associated with the y-intercept value, while k signifies the slope of the calibration curve).

sec.title: Sensing mechanism of N-CQDs toward CIP
sec.p: The observed FL enhancement of N-CQDs in the presence of CIP can be attributed to the synergistic interplay of hydrogen bonding and electron transfer mechanisms. The N-CQDs possess abundant surface functional groups, including –NH₂ and –COOH, which not only confer excellent aqueous solubility but also facilitate the formation of hydrogen bonds with CIP molecules. A conjugated system is established between N-CQDs and CIP, driven by the electron-accepting capability of quaternary amine groups on the N-CQDs and the electron-donating properties of CIP. Furthermore, as illustrated in Fig. 6e, the shoulder peaks of N-CQDs/CIP composite exhibit a distinct red shift relative to individual N-CQDs and CIP components, confirming the formation of a conjugated effect between the two constituents. As illustrated in Figure S2, the fluorescence lifetime of the N-CQDs/CIP system remains relatively unchanged compared to the original N-CQDs38. This dual interaction—hydrogen bonding and electron delocalization—collectively contributes to the concentration-dependent FL enhancement of the N-CQD-CIP system.

sec.title: Detection in real samples
sec.p: According to the national food safety standards, the residual amount of ciprofloxacin in honey must not exceed 100 µg/kg, making it essential to detect and quantify ciprofloxacin residues in honey. Compared with traditional analytical methods such as microbial inhibition assays, which suffer from high detection limits and poor specificity. Consequently, N-CQDs serving as an environmentally friendly carbon-based nanosensor with enhanced sensitivity and superior specificity, represent a viable alternative to conventional methods for accurate CIP quantification39. For practical applications, honey samples were spiked with CIP standard solutions at concentrations detailed in Table 1. The N-CQDs sensor exhibited recovery rates of 98.60–102.35%, indicating its utility as a cost-effective and eco-friendly carbon nanosensor for precise CIP quantification.

caption.p: Recovery rate of CIP in honey.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In this study, N-CQDs were synthesized through an eco-friendly hydrothermal approach using Solanum nigrum L. extract and triethylamine as dual carbon/nitrogen precursors. Comprehensive characterization via TEM, SEM, FT-IR, XPS and XRD confirmed the nanoscale morphology and surface functionalization of the N-CQDs. Significantly, the N-CQDs exhibited substantial antimicrobial efficacy against both S. aureus and E. coli bacterial strains, with MIC values of 1.2 mg/mL and 1.1 mg/mL, respectively. Moreover, the N-CQDs demonstrated pronounced fluorescence enhancement upon interaction with ciprofloxacin, displaying exceptional selectivity and sensitivity, with a calculated LOD of 316 nM. The feasibility of employing N-CQDs as fluorescent probes for ciprofloxacin detection was systematically validated through practical application in honey analysis. These findings highlight the potential of plant-derived N-CQDs as multifunctional nanomaterials for both environmental monitoring and antimicrobial applications.
